text.name: fh_alert_severe
text.text: Field %s (%s): severe threat – %s, the crop is dying. Spray: %s.

text.name: fh_alert_neighbour
text.text: Field %s (%s): %s – came from a neighbouring field. Spray: %s.

text.name: input_FH_MINIMAP_LAYER
text.text: Field Health – crop protection layer on the minimap

text.name: fh_settings_adminOnly
text.text: Only the admin can change these settings.

text.name: fh_setting_diseases_desc
text.text: Whether crop diseases are active. Off: no diseases appear, the ones on your fields disappear the next day and fungicide is not needed. Pests are not affected.

text.name: fh_setting_pests_desc
text.text: Whether pests are active. Off: no pests appear, the ones on your fields disappear the next day and insecticide is not needed. Diseases are not affected.

text.name: fh_setting_gracePeriod_desc
text.text: No new diseases or pests in the first years of the game, so you can get your farm going first. First year and First two years count by the year in the game calendar, so in an older savegame the calm start may already be over. Threats already on your fields develop as usual. Off: threats can appear from the start.

text.name: fh_setting_precisionFarming_desc
text.text: Whether the nitrogen, pH and soil maps of Precision Farming change the risk of threats. Off: the mod uses the basic field data of the game instead, as without Precision Farming. Without Precision Farming this setting changes nothing.

text.name: fh_setting_aiSprayNeeded_desc
text.text: On: AI helpers with fungicide or insecticide spray only growing crops of fields that are not protected yet and spots with threats, the rest counts as done, which saves product. Off: they spray the whole field, like with any other liquid.

text.name: fh_setting_preSowingSpray_desc
text.text: On: spraying fungicide or insecticide after the harvest, before you sow, protects the new crop. Off: only spraying done one day before sowing or later protects the new crop.

text.name: fh_setting_oneSpray_desc
text.text: On: spraying fungicide or insecticide cures and protects the field against diseases and pests at once, so one pass is enough. Off: fungicide only works against diseases and insecticide only against pests.

text.name: fh_setting_fieldInfoRisk_desc
text.text: Whether the field info box shows the disease and pest risk of the field and its main cause. Off: only threats and protection are shown, so the box stays shorter.

text.name: fh_setting_enabled_desc
text.text: Switches Field Health on or off. Off: no new diseases or pests appear, the existing ones stop developing and destroying crops, the field info box, the field details on the map and the minimap show nothing of the mod, and AI helpers spray like without it. The data of your fields is kept, so everything continues when you switch the mod on again.

text.name: fh_setting_diseaseChance_desc
text.text: Base chance that a normally farmed field gets a disease during one season (from sowing to harvest). It is only a starting point: good farming (manure, catch crops, crop rotation, right pH and nitrogen) lowers it, neglect (no fertilizer, monoculture, no plowing, acidic soil) raises it several times. Spraying fungicide before a disease appears reduces it to zero until harvest. 0% turns diseases off.

text.name: fh_setting_pestChance_desc
text.text: Base chance that pests appear on a normally farmed field during one season. Farming changes it: weeds, monoculture and no plowing raise it, catch crops and crop rotation lower it. Spraying insecticide before pests appear reduces it to zero until harvest. 0% turns pests off.

text.name: fh_setting_careInfluence_desc
text.text: How strongly the way you farm (fertilizing, soil work, crop rotation, catch crops, weeds, Precision Farming data) changes the base chances. None – only the base chance counts and all fields are equal. Low – mild differences. Normal (recommended) – good farming clearly pays off. High – neglected fields get sick very often, well kept ones almost never.

text.name: fh_setting_weatherInfluence_desc
text.text: How strongly the weather of the last days (temperature and rain) changes the chance of threats. Fungal diseases like rain and moisture, most pests like warm, dry weather, and every threat has its own temperature range. None – the weather does not count. Low – small differences. Normal (recommended) – clear differences. High – in favourable weather threats appear much more often, in unfavourable weather hardly at all.

text.name: fh_setting_stubbleRisk_desc
text.text: Whether unmulched stubble after harvest raises the risk (mainly of corn borer and diseases surviving on residues). It counts only after a harvest on the field and when the field was not plowed. Tramlines and paths across the field never count as stubble. Off – stubble does not change the risk at all.

text.name: fh_setting_fodderCrops
text.text: Threats on meadows and fodder crops

text.name: fh_setting_fodderCrops_desc
text.text: Whether meadows, grass, clover and alfalfa can get diseases and pests. Off (recommended) – these crops never get threats, and threats already on them disappear the next day. On – clover and alfalfa can get aphids; meadows and grass still never do.

text.name: fh_setting_fieldInfo_desc
text.text: Whether the field info box shows the threats, risk and protection of the field. Off – the box looks as without the mod; the map and the minimap still show the fields.

text.name: fh_setting_progression_desc
text.text: How fast an untreated threat reaches the next stage: low, then medium, then severe. Slow – every game month, Normal – every half month, Fast – every quarter month (at least one day). Only the severe stage destroys crops, so a slower pace gives you more time to spray.

text.name: fh_setting_spread_desc
text.text: How large a part of the field an untreated threat can cover. Small – up to 2.5%, Medium – up to 5%, Large – up to 10% of the field area. A patch grows unevenly at its edge, and now and then a new, smaller patch appears next to it – usually on the side the wind blows to that day. Spraying removes the threat completely.

text.name: fh_setting_patchSize_desc
text.text: How large the patches are in which a new threat appears and grows. Every patch has an irregular shape and a random size – small ones are more common than large ones. Small – patches usually 5–12 m across, Normal – 8–20 m, Large – 12–30 m. On small fields patches are always smaller.

text.name: fh_setting_neighbourSpread_desc
text.text: Whether a threat at the edge of a field can move to a neighbouring player field. This only happens when the fields touch or are separated by a very narrow strip, when the other field has a crop the threat attacks in the right growth stage, and when the other field is not sprayed. Pests move more often than diseases, and only from the medium stage on. NPC fields are never affected. Off, Rarely, Sometimes, Often – no, half, normal and double chance.

text.name: fh_setting_damage_desc
text.text: How much crop a severe threat destroys every day. Destroyed spots give nothing at harvest. Off – threats are only visible, the yield stays the same. Low, Normal, High – 1, 3 or 6 patches of a few meters per day, always only inside the infected area.

text.name: fh_setting_protectionThreshold_desc
text.text: How much of a field must be sprayed so that the whole field is protected against that kind of threat (diseases or pests). With less coverage a threat can still appear, but only on the unsprayed parts – sprayed areas are always protected. Default 90%. A lower threshold forgives missed corners and wedges, a higher one needs exact spraying.

text.name: fh_setting_protectionDuration_desc
text.text: How long fungicide and insecticide protect a field. Until harvest – one spraying with each product protects the field for the whole season (easiest). 2 months, 1 month, half a month – protection ends this long after the last spraying of the field and you have to spray again, like on a real farm.

text.name: fh_setting_fungicideUsage_desc
text.text: How much fungicide a sprayer uses per hectare. 100% is about 290 litres of mixture per hectare (the same as herbicide), which is one 1 l bottle per hectare. A lower rate makes spraying cheaper with less refilling, a higher one makes it more expensive. The effect of spraying is always the same. The change applies at once, even while working.

text.name: fh_setting_insecticideUsage_desc
text.text: How much insecticide a sprayer uses per hectare. 100% is about 290 litres of mixture per hectare (the same as herbicide), which is one 1 l bottle per 5 hectares. A lower rate makes spraying cheaper with less refilling, a higher one makes it more expensive. The effect of spraying is always the same. The change applies at once, even while working.

text.name: fh_setting_fungicidePrice_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 1 l bottle of fungicide. A bottle is enough for 1 hectare (290 l of spray mixture). Default 50. The game converts currencies 1:1. The price per litre of mixture follows this price, e.g. when buying the liquid at a station. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_insecticidePrice_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 1 l bottle of insecticide. A bottle is enough for 5 hectares (1450 l of spray mixture). Default 80. The game converts currencies 1:1. The price per litre of mixture follows this price, e.g. when buying the liquid at a station. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_fungicideCanisterPrice_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 5 l canister of fungicide. A canister is enough for 5 hectares (1450 l of spray mixture). Default 220, cheaper per litre than five 1 l bottles, like at a real dealer. The game converts currencies 1:1. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_insecticideCanisterPrice_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 5 l canister of insecticide. A canister is enough for 25 hectares (7250 l of spray mixture). Default 350, cheaper per litre than five 1 l bottles, like at a real dealer. The game converts currencies 1:1. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_fungicideCanister20Price_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 20 l canister of fungicide. A canister is enough for 20 hectares (5800 l of spray mixture). Default 800, the cheapest per litre of all containers. The game converts currencies 1:1. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_insecticideCanister20Price_desc
text.text: Shop price of one 20 l canister of insecticide. A canister is enough for 100 hectares (29,000 l of spray mixture). Default 1200, the cheapest per litre of all containers. The game converts currencies 1:1. The change applies at once in the shop.

text.name: fh_setting_farmLimit_desc
text.text: Maximum number of new threats on all fields of your farm per game year. Unlimited – every field has its own chance. Set for example 1 or 2 if you have many fields and want diseases and pests to be rare.

text.name: fh_setting_notifications_desc
text.text: Shows a message when a disease or pests appear on your field and when a threat becomes severe and starts destroying the crop. The message names the field, the crop, the threat and the product to spray.

text.name: fh_function_fungicideBottle
text.text: 1 l bottle of concentrate, rate 1 l/ha. Enough for 1 ha, which is 290 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against all diseases. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_function_insecticideBottle
text.text: 1 l bottle of concentrate, rate 0.2 l/ha. Enough for 5 ha, which is 1450 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against pests: aphids, leaf beetles, pollen beetles, potato beetles, corn borer and wireworms. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_function_fungicideCanister
text.text: 5 l canister of concentrate, rate 1 l/ha. Enough for 5 ha, which is 1450 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against all diseases. Cheaper per litre than the 1 l bottles. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_function_insecticideCanister
text.text: 5 l canister of concentrate, rate 0.2 l/ha. Enough for 25 ha, which is 7250 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against pests. Cheaper per litre than the 1 l bottles. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_function_fungicideCanister20
text.text: 20 l canister of concentrate, rate 1 l/ha. Enough for 20 ha, which is 5800 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against all diseases. Cheapest per litre, for large farms. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_function_insecticideCanister20
text.text: 20 l canister of concentrate, rate 0.2 l/ha. Enough for 100 ha, which is 29,000 l of spray mixture. Protects crops against pests. Cheapest per litre, for large farms. Put it next to a sprayer and fill the sprayer from it.

text.name: fh_help_intro_02
text.text: Field Health brings the crop diseases and pests that farmers deal with every day into the game. They appear on the fields of your farm during the season, develop and – if you do not fight them – destroy part of the crop. Two products from the shop fight them: fungicide against diseases and insecticide against pests. The mod is realistic but forgiving for casual play: a threat never covers the whole field, crop is destroyed only in the most severe stage, and one well-done spraying with each product protects the field until the end of the season.

text.name: fh_help_intro_04
text.text: 1. Sowing starts the crop season. From that day the infection pressure on the field grows – fastest in the time of year and growth stage in which a threat attacks, in weather that suits it and on a neglected field. 2. When the pressure passes the threshold rolled for the field, a patch of a disease or pests appears. You get a notification with the field number and the product to spray. 3. An untreated threat gets one stage worse every half month and slowly spreads. In the severe stage it destroys crop in small patches every day. 4. Spraying removes the threat and protects the sprayed spots. A field sprayed almost completely is immune to that kind of threat until harvest. 5. Harvest ends the season: threats and protection disappear, and the harvested crop becomes the previous crop of the next one.

text.name: fh_help_intro_06
text.text: Default values. The admin can change each of them in the settings (last column).

text.name: fh_help_intro_09
text.text: – Field info box (while you are on a field): threats with their severity, the risk and its main cause, the field's protection. – Map (ESC > Map > Crop protection): five layers – protection, diseases, pests, disease types and pest types. – Minimap: switch the layer with Left Alt + \. – Notifications: about a new threat, about the severe stage and about a threat that came from a neighbouring field. A sick crop looks normal in the game, so you see threats only in these places, not on the plants. Short tips at the bottom of the screen guide you through it step by step (you can turn them off in the settings).

text.name: fh_help_origin_01
text.text: Every player field with a growing crop can get at most one disease and one kind of pest per season. NPC fields, poplar and catch crops never get threats; meadows, grass, clover and alfalfa only when enabled in the settings. Bananas and coffee from the Beans & Alpacas DLC have diseases of their own in the DLC, so the mod leaves them alone. A threat does not appear on a random day. Every day the mod works out the infection pressure on the field and adds it to the sum of the days before. At the start of the season the field gets a random resistance threshold – when the sum of the pressure passes it, the field gets infected. That is why a threat appears early in one season, late in another and not at all in a third. The admin can also switch off threats for chosen crops in the “Crops” section of the settings.

text.name: fh_help_origin_03
text.text: 1. The base chance from the settings – by default 15% for a disease and 10% for pests over a season. 2. The field's risk, i.e. how you farm it: fertilizing, soil work, crop rotation and weeds (page “How you farm”). 3. How common the threat is – common diseases and pests appear much more often than rare ones (pages “Diseases” and “Pests”). 4. The time of year and the growth stage – outside its time a threat does not attack at all (page “Seasons and growth stages”). 5. The weather of the last days – rain helps fungal diseases, warmth and drought help most pests (page “Weather”).

text.name: fh_help_origin_05
text.text: This is how the field's risk changes the chance of a threat over the whole season with the default settings:

text.name: fh_help_origin_07
text.text: The table applies to a crop with an average set of threats that grows through all of their time. Crops attacked by many common diseases or pests get them more often (up to 1.4 times), crops with few threats less often (down to 0.5 times):

text.name: fh_help_origin_10
text.text: When an infection happens, the mod picks one of the threats that can attack the crop on that day. The chance of each is in proportion to its pressure of the day: how common it is times the field's risk, the time of year and the weather. Example: on wheat in May in rainy weather septoria or mildew appear most often, while stem rust, which is rare and likes heat, almost never does.

text.name: fh_help_origin_12
text.text: If at the moment of the infection the field is sprayed with the right product on at least 90% of its area, the infection fails and the field gets no threat of that kind this season. With less coverage the threat can appear, but only on the parts that were not sprayed. You don't have to spray in advance, though: spraying after the notification is enough too, because the crop only dies in the severe stage.

text.name: fh_help_timing_01
text.text: Every disease and every pest has its time: it attacks only in certain months and only in certain growth stages of the crop. Within that time it has a peak, when it is most dangerous. Outside its time a threat does not appear at all – it cannot come from a neighbouring field either.

text.name: fh_help_timing_04
text.text: The mod reads the stage from the crop's growth state in the game: the first 20% of the growing time are emergence, up to 45% leaf development and tillering, up to 70% stem elongation or budding, then heading and flowering, and a crop that is ready to harvest is ripe. Months follow the game calendar (the first period of the year is March), so the days per period do not change when threats attack.

text.name: fh_help_timing_06
text.text: The main months are those in which the pressure of the group of threats on the crop is highest. Check the map more often in that time. Spraying shortly before them prevents most infections, but it is not necessary: spraying after the notification is enough.

text.name: fh_help_farming_01
text.text: The field's risk is a multiplier of the infection pressure that comes from how you farm the field. The mod works it out for every threat separately; the field info box shows the highest disease and pest risk and the main cause. The multipliers in the tables multiply with each other, and the result always stays between 0.3 and 5.

text.name: fh_help_farming_07
text.text: The values are for a completely neglected field – partial neglect raises the risk in proportion. Only field work enabled in the game settings counts: without required plowing, not plowing changes nothing. The mod checks the field at 36 points and only where the crop grows, so tramlines and paths across the field do not count as neglect. Stubble and rolling count as missing only when three quarters of the field lack them. Stubble counts only after a harvest on this field and not after plowing (the setting “Risk from stubble” switches it off completely). In FS25 weeds do not grow after plowing.

text.name: fh_help_farming_10
text.text: The setting “Influence of farming” strengthens or weakens all these factors at once. None – every field has risk 1. Low – the differences are about half as large. Normal – as in the tables. High – the differences are half as large again.

text.name: fh_help_weather_01
text.text: Every in-game hour the mod reads the temperature and whether it rains. At the end of the day it works out the mean temperature of the day and the share of rainy hours. Wetness has a memory: half of it comes from the last day and half from the days before, because leaves stay wet long after rain. Every threat has a weather profile – a temperature range and how it deals with rain.

text.name: fh_help_weather_03
text.text: A temperature outside the range lowers the pressure to 0.4 times, a temperature in the optimum raises it to 1.2 times. Rain changes the pressure from 0.4 to 1.8 times – up for threats that like moisture, down for those that like drought. Together the weather changes the pressure from 0.2 to 2.5 times. Example multipliers after a few days of such weather (red – the threat grows, green – it shrinks):

text.name: fh_help_weather_05
text.text: The setting “Influence of weather”: None – the weather does not count, Low – milder multipliers, Normal – as in the table, High – stronger. After a few warm, rainy days in summer watch potatoes and heading cereals in particular, and in a dry, hot summer – pests.

text.name: fh_help_diseases_01
text.text: Fungicide fights all diseases. The tables show how common a disease is, which crops it attacks, in which months it appears and when it is worst, in which growth stage it does the most damage and what helps it.

text.name: fh_help_diseases_07
text.text: Crops of maps that the mod does not know can get grey mould and aphids. Onions of the Highlands Fishing Expansion and of mods are recognised automatically.

text.name: fh_help_pests_01
text.text: Insecticide fights all pests. The columns of the tables mean the same as on the page “Diseases”.

text.name: fh_help_progress_01
text.text: A new threat is one or two irregular patches with a frayed edge and healthy gaps inside. It starts in the low stage. If you do not fight it, it goes through these steps:

text.name: fh_help_progress_03
text.text: Destroyed crop does not grow back and yields nothing at harvest, but only the severe stage destroys it, in small patches. Until then the sick crop looks normal. So you don't have to spray in advance: spraying after the notification is enough, because at the default pace the severe stage comes after about a game month or later. Spraying in any stage removes the threat completely from the sprayed spots.

text.name: fh_help_spraying_01
text.text: The products are made by the company Opryskex: the fungicide Grzybobój 250 EC (green label) and the insecticide Robalex 100 CS (red label). When buying you can choose the MST brand (Mafia Solec Team) instead: Solectop 280 SC and Mafiozol 50 EW. They work the same, only the label differs. You buy them in the shop in 1 l bottles and in 5 l and 20 l canisters. Put the container next to the sprayer and fill it as from a pallet. The game does not mix the concentrate with water, so the content of a container is all the spray mixture it makes. The bigger the container, the cheaper per hectare.

text.name: fh_help_spraying_06
text.text: – Spray one day before sowing at the earliest, because sowing and harvest remove older protection. Earlier spraying only counts with the setting “Spraying before sowing”. – Fungicide does not protect against pests and insecticide not against diseases. Full protection needs both. With the setting “One spray for both” one of them is enough. – Missed wedges and headlands count: below 90% coverage a threat can appear on unsprayed strips. – The products do not fertilize and do not kill weeds. – With a shorter spray protection (setting) the protection of the whole field ends that long after the last spraying.

text.name: fh_help_map_02
text.text: While you are on a field, the field info box shows: – Disease and Pests: the active threat and its severity (low, medium, severe), – Disease risk and Pest risk: low, normal, elevated or high, and from elevated on also the main cause, – Disease protection and Pest protection: how much of the field is sprayed, – a hint which product fights the threat.

text.name: fh_help_map_04
text.text: In ESC > Map choose the page “Crop protection”. Below its title a second selector with arrows switches between five layers. Clicking a legend entry hides it on the map. Only fields of your farm with a growing crop are shown. Click a farmland to see the threats and the protection of its fields. Fields with a crop that cannot get threats (e.g. meadows, grass and catch crops, or a crop switched off in the settings) are not shown, and on a field split into several crops only the part with the season's crop is shown.

text.name: fh_help_map_09
text.text: Left Alt + \ switches the minimap layer: protection, diseases, pests and no layer. You can change the keys during the game in ESC > Settings > Controls, entry “Field Health – crop protection layer on the minimap” (the main menu does not list mod keys, because mods are loaded with the savegame). When you spray fungicide or insecticide while the minimap layer is off, the protection layer turns on by itself and goes off a few seconds after you turn the sprayer off. If you press the key while spraying, your choice stays.

text.name: fh_help_pf_01
text.text: With Precision Farming, Field Health works as its extension and uses its soil maps. Instead of fertilizing in general the nitrogen compared with the target counts, and instead of liming in general the soil pH.

text.name: fh_help_pf_03
text.text: The best protection is the same work you do for the yield: fertilizing to the target, liming to the optimal pH and catch crops. The console command fhPrecisionFarming writes to the log how the mod reads Precision Farming data.

text.name: fh_help_settings_01
text.text: You find the mod settings in ESC > Settings, in a tab of their own called “Field Health”, divided into sections. They are saved with the savegame. Every player can see them, but in multiplayer only the admin can change them (on a dedicated server, log in as admin first). Move over an option to see its description. The “Crops” section switches off threats for chosen crops of the map. The “Tips” section is separate for every player and is not stored in the savegame: it turns the short tips at the bottom of the screen on or off, sets how often they come and lets you start them over.

text.name: fh_help_tips_02
text.text: 1. Fertilize as needed, lime and do not sow the same crop two years in a row. Sow a catch crop between main crops. 2. You don't have to spray in advance, spraying after the notification is enough (point 4). If you prefer to be safe, spray the field with fungicide and insecticide before the main months of the threats (page “Seasons and growth stages”). Once per season is enough if you cover at least 90% of the field. 3. Check the “Protection” layer on the map – green fields are protected against both kinds of threats. 4. After a notification spray the named field with the named product before the threat reaches the severe stage. 5. An AI worker with fungicide or insecticide sprays unprotected fields completely and protected ones only where a threat is. 6. Lots of fields? Set “Threat limit per farm” or turn on “One spray for both”, and switch off crops that should not get threats in the “Crops” section.

text.name: fh_help_tips_04
text.text: – Monoculture and no plowing are the most common causes of high risk, e.g. wheat after wheat without plowing helps septoria, tan spot and fusarium. – Maize before wheat clearly raises the risk of fusarium, grassland before potatoes the risk of wireworms. – Slurry and liquid fertilizer give lush growth, which mildew, rusts and aphids like. – A rainy summer is the time of late blight, septoria and fusarium, a dry and hot one the time of aphids, potato beetles, thrips and cutworms. – Canola has two dangerous times: autumn (flea beetles, turnip sawfly, phoma) and spring (stem weevils, pollen beetles, sclerotinia). – A threat in the medium or severe stage can move to a touching player field.

text.name: fh_help_admin_04
text.text: – The simulation runs on the server and players see its results. The settings and the commands fhSet, fhClear and fhDailyTick are for the admin only. – Notifications go to the players of the farm that owns the field, each in their own language. – The mod saves its data only in two files of its own in the savegame folder: fieldHealth.xml and fieldHealthMap.grle. It can be removed safely – the game skips these files, and only the bottles and canisters of the products disappear from the map. – Savegames of an earlier version of the mod are converted to the new format when loaded. – Onions of the Highlands Fishing Expansion and of mods are recognised automatically – the log says so. – Do not use another crop disease mod (e.g. Crop Diseases) at the same time – Field Health warns about it in the log. Each player's tip history is kept in their game profile (modSettings/FS25_FieldHealth/tips.xml), not in the savegame.

text.name: fh_help_admin_06
text.text: Field Health – author: MatrikSky. Idea inspired by the mod “Crop Diseases” by BMP. The bottle model is based on “fertilizer Bottle” by shabanimate, the canister model on “#6 Plastic Canister” by hoxsvl (both CC BY 4.0, sketchfab.com).

text.name: fh_setting_crop_desc
text.text: Off: this crop never gets threats. Threats already on it disappear the next day and its fields are not shown on the protection map.

text.name: fh_setting_tips_desc
text.text: Short tips for beginners at the bottom of the screen. This setting is yours only and applies to every savegame.

text.name: fh_setting_tipsFrequency_desc
text.text: How often the next tip of the list appears. Tips about what you are doing right now come at once.

text.name: fh_setting_tipsReset_desc
text.text: All tips appear again, starting with the first one.

text.name: fh_tips_resetQuestion
text.text: All tips will appear again, starting with the first one. Do you want to do this?

text.name: fh_tip_welcome
text.text: Field Health brings the crop diseases and pests that farmers deal with every day onto your fields, from septoria and fusarium to Colorado potato beetles and pollen beetles. Each threat attacks certain crops and has its own season and favourite weather, and how likely it is to appear depends largely on your farming practice. When a new pathogen or pest appears on one of your fields, you get a notification and a tip that describes it. The full guide with tables is in the game's help, and you can turn the tips off in the settings, on the Field Health tab.

text.name: fh_tip_products
text.text: Fungicide controls diseases and insecticide controls pests. You buy both in the shop, in the section with fertilizers and herbicide, in bottles of one litre or in canisters of five and twenty litres, and the larger the pack, the lower the cost of a treatment per hectare. The insecticide rate is five times lower than the fungicide rate, so a bottle of fungicide covers roughly one hectare and a bottle of insecticide about five.

text.name: fh_tip_whenToSpray
text.text: You don't need to spray in advance, because a treatment after the threat notification is quite enough. A new outbreak starts in the low stage and only destroys crop in the severe stage, so you usually have time to react without any yield loss. An untreated outbreak slowly spreads, and from the medium stage on it can move to a neighbouring field if the two fields touch. A preventive treatment before the main months of the threats makes sense on fields with a high risk, because a field sprayed before the infection is immune to it.

text.name: fh_tip_protection
text.text: A treatment kills the pathogen or pest on the sprayed spots at once and protects them against new infections of the same kind, by default until harvest. A field only counts as protected once at least %s percent of its area is covered, so headlands and wedges count too. Fungicide protects against diseases and insecticide against pests, unless the option %s is turned on in the settings. A field can have at most one disease and one pest per season, so after a successful treatment it stays free of that kind of threat until harvest.

text.name: fh_tip_settings
text.text: In the settings, on the Field Health tab, you adjust the mod to your style of play, from the chances of threats and how fast they develop to the prices of the products. On a large farm the option %s comes in handy, as it limits the number of new threats on all fields per year. When you turn on %s, a treatment with one product is enough, because fungicide and insecticide then protect against diseases and pests at once. In the %s section you switch off threats for chosen crops, and in multiplayer all these settings are changed by the admin.

text.name: fh_tip_sprayerReady
text.text: Your sprayer holds fungicide, which controls diseases and protects the sprayed spots against new infections. Before you head out, check on the map, on the %s page, which fields have a disease or no protection against diseases yet. A healthy and protected field needs no further treatment, so don't waste product on it.

text.name: fh_tip_spraying
text.text: While you treat, keep an eye on the minimap, because the protection layer shows the sprayed spots as you go, and if no layer was on before, it appears by itself. Only the area that actually received spray liquid counts, so avoid strips between passes and don't skip the headlands. A field only counts as protected once at least %s percent of its area is covered.

text.name: fh_tip_severe
text.text: One of the threats on your fields has reached the severe stage and is starting to destroy the crop in small patches, where the plants die and bare soil is left. You find the field number in the notification, so treat that field as soon as possible, because destroyed crop does not grow back and gives no yield. Spraying stops the losses at once, and the rest of the crop goes on developing normally.

text.name: fh_setting_stageProtection_desc
text.text: From the chosen growth stage on, the crop is protected without spraying. No new threats appear on it, and threats already there stop developing and no longer destroy crop. By default a crop ready to harvest is protected, because nobody sprays such a field.

text.name: fh_tip_monitoring
text.text: An infected crop looks just like a healthy one in the game, and the damage only shows in the severe stage, when plants die off in small patches. The field info box shows the state of a field, with the active threat and its stage, the disease and pest risk with its main cause and the share of the field that has been sprayed. You see all your fields at once on the %s map page, which has layers for protection, diseases, pests and threat types. You can also turn on the protection layer on the minimap, and while you treat a field it appears by itself.

text.name: fh_tip_farming
text.text: The risk of infection depends largely on your farming practice. Monoculture and growing without plowing favour diseases that survive on crop residues, such as septoria and tan spot, and wheat after maize is particularly prone to fusarium. Slurry and quickly available nitrogen give a lush crop that mildew, rusts and aphids love. Liming, manure and catch crops reduce diseases that live in the soil, such as sclerotinia, while plowing, rolling and catch crops reduce soil pests such as wireworms, which are most numerous after grassland. Weeds favour pests that breed on them, such as aphids and pollen beetles.

text.name: fh_tip_weather
text.text: The pressure of diseases and pests changes with the weather of the last few days. A warm and rainy summer favours late blight, fusarium and Cercospora leaf spot, while a cool and wet spring favours septoria, Rhynchosporium and net blotch. In a dry and hot summer aphids, Colorado potato beetles, thrips and cutworms develop fastest, whereas yellow rust and snow mould prefer the cold. After a few days of favourable weather, scout your fields more often, especially cereals at heading and potatoes in midsummer.

text.name: fh_tip_aiHelper
text.text: An AI helper with fungicide or insecticide only treats where a treatment is needed. It sprays a field without protection completely, and on a field that is already protected only the outbreaks, so it does not waste product on healthy areas. If you would rather have it spray the whole field every time, you can change that in the settings.

text.name: fh_tip_sprayerReady_pest
text.text: Your sprayer holds insecticide, which controls pests and protects the sprayed spots against new infestations. Before you head out, check on the map, on the %s page, on which fields pests are feeding and which have no protection against them yet. A healthy and protected field needs no further treatment, so don't waste product on it.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_cereal_mildew
text.text: Cereal powdery mildew is a fungal disease caused by Blumeria graminis that attacks wheat, barley, rye, triticale, oats and spelt. It forms a white, powdery coating of mycelium on leaves and leaf sheaths, which later turns grey and reduces photosynthesis. It develops most strongly in May and June, during tillering and stem elongation, at moderate temperatures and even without rain. A lush crop after slurry and quickly available nitrogen favours it, and it is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_septoria
text.text: Septoria leaf blotch is caused by the fungus Zymoseptoria tritici, one of the most damaging pathogens of wheat, triticale and spelt. Long brown lesions with black fruiting bodies appear on the leaves, and raindrops splash the spores from the lower leaves up to the upper ones. The disease is most dangerous in May and June, from stem elongation to flowering, when it is cool and wet. The fungus survives on crop residues, so no plowing and unmulched stubble raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_brown_rust
text.text: Brown rust is a fungal disease of wheat, triticale, spelt and rye caused by fungi of the genus Puccinia. It forms small, rusty brown pustules of spores on the leaves that rub off easily on your finger and spread quickly with the wind. It is most dangerous in June, at heading and flowering, in warm weather with dew or passing showers. The risk rises in a lush crop after slurry and quickly available nitrogen, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_fusarium
text.text: Fusarium head blight and ear rot are caused by fungi of the genus Fusarium that attack cereals, millet, maize and sorghum. Infection happens at flowering, and infected grain is small and shrivelled, often with a pink coating, and contains mycotoxins such as deoxynivalenol. It is most dangerous in June and July, when flowering falls in warm and rainy weather. The fungi overwinter on crop residues, which makes wheat after maize without plowing a textbook example of high risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_net_blotch
text.text: Net blotch is caused by the fungus Pyrenophora teres and threatens both winter and spring barley. Brown lesions crossed by a dark net of dead tissue appear on the leaves, merge over time and dry out. The disease develops from early spring, most strongly in May, during tillering and stem elongation, in cool and damp weather. The fungus survives on crop residues, so barley after barley and no plowing raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_snow_mould
text.text: Snow mould is caused by the fungus Microdochium nivale and attacks winter cereals in winter and early spring. It develops under snow that lies for a long time and in cold, damp weather, and infected plants are covered with a greyish white or pinkish mycelium and die off in patches. It is most dangerous in February and March, while the plants are still young. Overly lush stands after slurry and quickly available nitrogen favour it, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_sclerotinia
text.text: Sclerotinia stem rot is caused by the fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, which attacks canola, mustard, sunflower, soybeans, pulses, potatoes and carrots. Pale, wet lesions with white mycelium form on the stems, and black sclerotia develop inside them that survive in the soil for several years. Most infections happen in May and June, at flowering, in warm and humid weather. The risk rises after canola, sunflower and pulses and on acidic soil, while liming, manure and catch crops reduce it. The disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_alternaria
text.text: Alternaria is a group of diseases caused by fungi of the genus Alternaria that attack potatoes, carrots, parsnips, canola, mustard, sunflower and onions. Dark brown spots with clear concentric rings form on the leaves and, on canola, also on the pods. It is most dangerous in July and August, towards the end of the season, in warm weather with dew at night. The fungi survive on crop residues, so no plowing and unmulched stubble raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_late_blight
text.text: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, an organism similar to fungi, and is the most dangerous disease of potatoes. Quickly growing, watery lesions that turn brown appear on the leaves with a white coating underneath, and the disease also spreads to stems and tubers. It is most dangerous from June to August, when rain follows warm days and the crop stays wet for a long time. In a rainy summer scout your potatoes especially often, and control the disease with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_cercospora
text.text: Cercospora leaf spot, caused by the fungus Cercospora beticola, is the most important leaf disease of sugar beet and beetroot and also attacks spinach. Small, round, grey spots with a reddish brown border form on the leaves, and infected leaves dry out, which lowers root yield and sugar content. It is most dangerous in July and August, in hot weather with high humidity. The fungus overwinters on leaf residues, so beet after beet and no plowing raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_grey_mould
text.text: Grey mould is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea, which attacks many crops, among them sunflower, pulses, spinach, buckwheat, onions and grapes, and in Field Health also crops the mod does not know. A grey, dusty coating of spores appears on flowers, fruit and pods, and the infected tissue rots. It is most dangerous in July and August, from flowering to harvest, in cool and rainy weather. A dense, lush crop after slurry favours it, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_yellow_rust
text.text: Yellow rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia striiformis, which attacks wheat, triticale and spelt. It forms the typical yellow stripes of spore pustules along the leaf veins, and in a heavy infection the leaves dry out quickly. Unlike other rusts it likes the cold, so it is most dangerous in April and May, during stem elongation. A lush crop after slurry favours it, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_tan_spot
text.text: Tan spot is caused by a fungus of the genus Pyrenophora that attacks wheat, triticale and spelt. Oval, light brown spots with a yellow halo and a dark point in the middle form on the leaves. It is most dangerous in May and June, from stem elongation to flowering, in warm and humid weather. The fungus overwinters on straw and crop residues, which makes it a typical disease of wheat grown after wheat without plowing, and it is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_eyespot
text.text: Eyespot is caused by fungi of the genus Oculimacula that attack the stem base of wheat, triticale, barley and rye. Oval lesions shaped like an eye form on the lower part of the stem, and the weakened stems break, so the crop lodges. Infections happen in autumn and early spring, most often in April, during tillering and early stem elongation, in cool and damp weather. The fungi survive on straw residues, so cereals after cereals and no plowing raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_rhynchosporium
text.text: Rhynchosporium leaf scald is caused by fungi of the genus Rhynchosporium that attack barley, rye and triticale. Greyish green and later pale lesions with a dark brown border appear on the leaves, often where the leaf blade joins the sheath. It is most dangerous in April and May, during tillering and stem elongation, when it rains often and is cool. The pathogen survives on crop residues, so growing without plowing raises the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_ramularia
text.text: Ramularia leaf spot of barley is caused by a fungus of the genus Ramularia that attacks the crop late in its development. Small, rectangular brown spots bordered by the leaf veins appear on the upper leaves and awns, and the leaves die quickly, so the grain fills less well. It is most dangerous in June and July, after heading, when the damp lasts long after rain. It is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_stem_rust
text.text: Black stem rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia graminis, which appears rarely but can be very damaging. It forms long, dark rusty pustules of spores on stems and leaf sheaths that later turn black, and infected stems weaken and break. The disease attacks wheat, triticale, spelt, rye, barley and oats and is most dangerous in July, in hot weather, during heading and ripening. It is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_phoma
text.text: Phoma stem canker is caused by the fungus Leptosphaeria maculans, which attacks canola and mustard. Most infections happen in autumn, especially in October, when pale spots with black fruiting bodies appear on the young leaves, and the fungus then grows into the stem and makes it crack at the root collar. A cool and rainy autumn favours the infections. The spores come from crop residues, so canola after canola or other brassicas and no plowing raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_cylindrosporiosis
text.text: Light leaf spot is caused by the fungus Pyrenopeziza brassicae, a threat to canola and mustard in the cool part of the year. Pale green spots with small white clusters of spores appear on the leaves, and infected leaves turn yellow and die. Infections happen in autumn, especially in November, and in early spring, in March and April, while the plants form a leaf rosette. Crop residues and brassicas after brassicas raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_beet_mildew
text.text: Beet powdery mildew, caused by the fungus Erysiphe betae, attacks sugar beet and beetroot. The leaves are covered with a white, powdery coating, and badly infected leaves turn yellow and dry out, which lowers yield and sugar content. Unlike most fungal diseases it likes warm and dry weather, so it is most dangerous in July and August in a hot summer. Lush growth after slurry and quickly available nitrogen favours it, and it is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_ascochyta
text.text: Ascochyta blight is caused by fungi of the genus Ascochyta that attack peas and beans. Brown spots with a dark border form on leaves, stems and pods, and infected seeds are discoloured and germinate poorly. It is most dangerous in June, during flowering and pod set, in cool and rainy weather. The fungi survive on crop residues, so pulses after pulses and no plowing raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_downy_mildew
text.text: Downy mildew is caused by oomycetes of the genus Peronospora, organisms similar to fungi, which attack onions, spinach and peas. Pale spots that turn yellow appear on the leaves, with a violet grey coating of spores underneath or over the whole surface, and then the leaves die. It is most dangerous in June and July, when the nights are cool and the leaves stay wet from dew and rain for a long time. A dense, lush crop after slurry favours it, and it is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_corn_leaf_blight
text.text: Northern corn leaf blight is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum, which attacks maize and sorghum. Large, long, greyish brown lesions that can be over ten centimetres long appear on the leaves and reduce the leaf area. It is most dangerous in July and August, from tasselling on, in warm and humid weather. The fungus overwinters on maize residues, so maize after maize and residues that have not been mulched raise the risk, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_crown_rust
text.text: Oat crown rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia coronata and is the most important rust of this cereal. It forms bright orange, round pustules of spores on the leaves, and a heavy infection makes the leaves dry out early and lowers grain weight. It is most dangerous in June and July, at panicle emergence, in warm weather with dew. A lush crop after slurry favours it, and the disease is controlled with fungicide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_aphids
text.text: Aphids are small sucking insects that feed on almost all field crops, from cereals and maize to potatoes, beet, canola and pulses, and in Field Health also on crops the mod does not know. They suck sap from leaves and shoots, weaken the plants and transmit viruses, for example barley yellow dwarf virus. They are most numerous in May and June, in warm and dry weather, when their colonies grow very fast. Weeds and lush growth after slurry favour them, and they are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_leaf_beetle
text.text: Cereal leaf beetles, mainly Oulema melanopus and Oulema lichenis, are beetles whose larvae feed on cereal leaves. They scrape away the tissue between the veins and leave white, translucent stripes, and a badly damaged flag leaf costs a lot of yield. They do the most damage in May and June, from stem elongation to heading, in warm and dry weather. Weeds favour them, and they are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_pollen_beetle
text.text: Pollen beetles are small black beetles with a metallic sheen that feed in the flower buds of canola and mustard. They bite into the buds to get at the pollen, and damaged buds dry up and drop, leaving empty stalks on the shoots. They are most dangerous in April and May, at the bud stage before flowering, when the weather warms up. Weeds favour them, and they are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_potato_beetle
text.text: Colorado potato beetles are beetles with black stripes on yellow wing cases, and both larvae and adults eat potato leaves. The voracious reddish larvae can strip the plants bare, and without leaves the tubers stop growing. They do the most damage in June and July, in warm and dry weather, when new larvae keep hatching. The beetles overwinter in the soil, so potatoes after potatoes raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_corn_borer
text.text: The European corn borer is a moth whose caterpillars bore tunnels in the stalks and cobs of maize, sorghum and millet. Damaged stalks break, and the cobs are poorly formed and drop easily. The caterpillars feed mainly in July, during tasselling and flowering, in warm and dry weather. They overwinter in stalk residues and stubble, so maize after maize, no plowing and unmulched residues raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_wireworm
text.text: Wireworms are the yellow, hard larvae of click beetles and live in the soil for several years. They eat germinating seeds and young plants of maize, beet, onions and carrots, and they bore narrow tunnels in potato tubers that lower the quality of the crop. They are most dangerous in April and May, during emergence. They are most numerous after grassland and after pulses, and plowing, rolling and catch crops reduce their numbers, while the pest itself is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_stem_weevil
text.text: Rape stem weevils, mainly Ceutorhynchus napi and Ceutorhynchus pallidactylus, are small weevils that are the first pests to fly into canola and mustard in early spring. The females lay their eggs in the stems, and the larvae bore tunnels inside, so the stems crack, bend and break more easily. They are most dangerous in March and April, while the stem grows, once the temperature rises above a few degrees. The risk rises when canola or mustard follows other brassicas, and the pests are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_seed_weevil
text.text: The cabbage seed weevil is a grey weevil that attacks canola and mustard during flowering. The females lay their eggs in young pods, and the larvae eat the seeds inside. It is most numerous in May, at full flowering, in warm and sunny weather. Weeds favour it, and it is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_flea_beetle
text.text: Flea beetles are tiny jumping beetles that chew the typical round shot holes into cotyledons and young leaves. They attack emerging canola, mustard, beet and spinach, and in a heavy attack young plants can die while still at the cotyledon stage. They are most dangerous in May with spring sowings and in September, when winter canola emerges, especially in warm and dry weather. Weeds and brassicas after brassicas favour them, and they are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_turnip_sawfly
text.text: The turnip sawfly is a sawfly whose dark grey larvae look like caterpillars and eat the leaves of young canola and mustard. In large numbers they can leave nothing but the leaf veins within a few days. It is most dangerous from August to October, above all in September, when winter canola has only a few leaves. Weeds favour it, and it is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_frit_fly
text.text: The frit fly is a small black fly whose larvae feed inside the young shoots of cereals and maize. The larva bores into the centre of the shoot, so the youngest leaf turns yellow and dies, and the plant forms weak side shoots. In spring it attacks spring cereals and maize, most often in May and June, and in autumn early sown winter cereals, always at emergence and the first leaves. Weeds and growing after grassland favour it, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_wheat_midge
text.text: Wheat blossom midges are tiny orange or yellow flies whose larvae feed in the ears of wheat, triticale, spelt and rye. They suck sap from the developing grains, so the grain is small, shrivelled and lighter. The females lay their eggs in June, at heading, preferably on warm, muggy and still evenings. The larvae overwinter in the soil, so cereals after cereals raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_cutworm
text.text: Cutworms are moth caterpillars that hide in the soil by day and come out to feed at night. They bite through plants just at the soil surface and bore into beet, potatoes, carrots and onions, eating holes into them. They are most dangerous in July and August in a hot, dry summer, when the caterpillars are already large. Plowing, rolling, catch crops and weed control reduce their numbers, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_beet_fly
text.text: The mangold fly is a fly whose larvae mine the leaves of beet and spinach. They feed inside the leaf blade and eat the tissue, leaving pale, spreading blotches that later turn brown. The first generation does the most damage in May and June, when young beet has a few leaves and the weather is warm and humid. Weeds favour it, and it is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_onion_fly
text.text: The onion fly is a fly whose larvae feed in onion leaves and bulbs. Young plants turn yellow, wilt and are easy to pull out of the ground, and in older onions the larvae eat out the inside, so the bulbs rot. The first generation in May is the most dangerous, at emergence, in warm and humid weather. The pupae overwinter in the soil, so onions after onions and no plowing raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_thrips
text.text: Thrips are tiny, slender insects that suck sap from the leaves, flowers and pods of onions and pulses. Silvery, shiny patches appear on the leaves, and the damaged tissue dries up. They are most numerous in July and August, in a hot and dry summer, when several generations develop in a short time. Weeds favour them, and they are controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_carrot_fly
text.text: The carrot fly is a small fly whose larvae bore tunnels in the roots of carrots and parsnips. Damaged roots have rusty brown tunnels, rot easily and lose their market value. The pest has two generations, the first in May and the second in August, and attacks most readily in warm, humid weather. The pupae overwinter in the soil, so carrots or parsnips grown after each other and no plowing raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_pea_leaf_weevil
text.text: Pea leaf weevils are small greyish brown weevils that chew semicircular notches into the leaf margins of peas, beans and soybeans. Their larvae feed in the soil on the root nodules, so the plants fix less nitrogen from the air. They are most dangerous in May, at emergence and the first leaves, in a warm spring. The risk rises when pulses follow pulses, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_rootworm
text.text: The western corn rootworm is a beetle that appears rarely but is one of the most dangerous maize pests in the world. The larvae feed on the roots, so the plants lodge and bend into a shape resembling a goose neck, and the adult beetles damage the silks of the cobs. It does the most damage in July and August, at flowering, in a warm and dry summer. The eggs overwinter in the soil, so in maize monoculture the risk rises many times over and crop rotation is the best protection. The pest is controlled with insecticide.

text.name: fh_tipThreat_ground_beetle
text.text: The cereal ground beetle is a beetle that appears rarely but can locally destroy young cereal crops. The larvae live in vertical burrows in the soil and pull leaves into them at night, chewing them and leaving frayed remains that look like tow. It is most dangerous in autumn, especially in October, while winter cereals emerge, and less so in spring. Cereals after cereals and growing without plowing raise the risk, and the pest is controlled with insecticide.
